perf: N+1 queries on thing table causing 3.8M single-row DB lookups

Production pg_stat_statements showed SELECT-by-key as the database's highest-volume query with 3,830,328 calls in the observation window. The existing batched equivalent accounted for only 134,057 calls, a reported 28:1 ratio of unbatched to batched lookups. The issue explicitly diagnoses pages that resolve list items individually as an N+1 pattern and recommends replacing loops with the existing get_many batching path. The repeated single-row lookups consumed roughly 2.5 million milliseconds of database time and increased cache/I/O pressure on the production database.

Payment incidents can be caused by configuration changes rather than payment-provider capacity. Indicators include failures beginning immediately after a rollout, a narrow card, region, gateway, or authentication segment being affected, normal infrastructure health, and recovery after reverting configuration. Investigation should compare the active configuration with the previous known-good version, check routing, 3DS, firewall, merchant, and entitlement rules, and correlate failure codes with the changed scope. Treat rollback as a mitigation and add validation, staged rollout, and configuration-diff observability before retrying the change.

Incident Report: Running Dry on Memory Without Noticing

Honeycomb reported four roughly 20-minute ingest brownouts in which 1–3% of customer telemetry was rejected. The incident trigger was explicitly identified as a slow memory leak that accumulated over hours across ingest backends. The backends crashed within minutes of one another as memory pressure accumulated, causing in-flight and new ingest requests to fail. After the leak was identified, Honeycomb reverted the bad commit and deployed a fixed release; memory behavior and service health returned to normal.

GitLab Versions differ across zonal clusters

GitLab opened an incident because production component versions appeared out of sync across zonal clusters after deployment. Investigation determined the condition was a false alarm caused by stale metadata for a ContainerStatusUnknown pod whose containers had already exited. No traffic was reaching the lingering pod and GitLab explicitly reported no customer impact. Deleting the stale pod cleared the alert; the visible deployment/version disparity was therefore a distractor rather than an active service fault.

A database connection leak occurs when application code checks out a connection from a pool but fails to return it on every teardown path. Typical signals include an increasing count of checked-out connections, a pool that remains exhausted after request load falls, database-dependent requests timing out, and temporary recovery after process restart. Diagnose by comparing pool checkout and checkin counts, inspecting long-lived sessions, and tracing cancellation, streaming, exception, and retry paths. Repair requires guaranteed cleanup in finally blocks or context managers, bounded pool timeouts, and alerts on sustained pool saturation rather than only database CPU.

An N+1 query problem occurs when code fetches a collection and then performs an additional database query for each item. It appears as very high counts of similar single-row queries, latency increasing with list size, unnecessary network round trips, and database time dominated by repeated lookups. Confirm by tracing one request, grouping SQL by normalized statement, and comparing unbatched and batched call counts. Typical fixes are eager loading, joins, batch fetch APIs, prefetching, or restructuring the data-access layer so a list is resolved in a bounded number of queries.

A no-fault classification is appropriate when investigation shows the observed symptom does not represent a production defect in the diagnosed service. Examples include stale dashboards, version skew in monitoring, expected maintenance behavior, upstream test traffic, or an alert whose assumptions are wrong. The diagnosis should be supported by independent health signals, request traces, deployment state, and reproduction attempts. Closing as no-fault should still record why the alert fired and whether observability or alert logic needs correction so the same false positive does not repeatedly consume incident response time.

Payment Issues

ElevenLabs investigated payment-processing issues affecting ElevenAPI on April 22, 2026. The official update identified a billing-system misconfiguration that delayed subscription provisioning; error rates returned to baseline and full resolution was confirmed.

Incident: gitlab.git.nrw outage

git.nrw reported a complete GitLab outage lasting 5 hours 45 minutes. Database replication had silently stopped, leaving one database node to accumulate WAL transaction logs. The remaining database node's disk filled with WAL logs and the service went down. The incident was resolved by increasing disk capacity and restoring replication, with WAL-size monitoring added as follow-up.
